newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan rules out cancelling power purchase deal.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan rules out cancelling power purchase deal.

text.p: Pakistan Water and Power Minister Nisar Ali Khan said on Sunday there was no plan to terminate a power purchase agreement with the largest private electricity generator, Hub Power Co Ltd (Hubco).
On Friday, Hubco received notice from WAPDA threatening to terminate the power purchase agreement within 30 days.
WAPDA said it was taking the action because the seal on one of the two meters installed at Hubco to measure electricity transmitted to the national grid was damaged in March.
Khan told Reuters by telephone the state-run Water and Power Development Authority's (WAPDA) threat of ending the agreement with Hubco was an over-reaction by an "over-zealous low-level" official.
"Although a breach did occur, and it was serious enough to warrant a notice to Hubco, there was no need to send a notice threatening to terminate the power purchase agreement," he said.
"I am sure the matter will be amicably resolved in the next couple of days. I expect the two sides will meet on Tuesday."
Hubco denied any wrongdoing, saying the matter did not affect the integrity of the system for recording electricity supplied and did not provide grounds for termination of the agreement.
Anisur Rehman, research head at SocGen Crosby Securities, told Reuters that termination of the power purchase agreement could badly affect furture foreign investment in Pakistan.
"Any attempt to renegotiate (power) tariffs or undermine in any way foreign interest can have an exteremly bad effect on further foreign investment in Pakistan," Rehman said.
Local newspapers have been casting a critical spotlight on power purchase agreements signed with more than two dozen private power companies by the government of former prime minister Benazir Bhutto.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif sparked the debate by setting up a committee last month to review the agreements and seek ways of reducing the tariffs payable to the private power firms.
"The incident basically reduces the credibility of the government policy and its ability to implement it," Kalim Aziz, head of research at ING Baring Securities, said.
"It highlights lack of coordination with the government at a time when it cannot afford to mismanage investor relations."
Khan was quoted by Pakistani newspapers as saying the government did not want to create a hostile or unfriendly environment for investment in Pakistan.
"But I want to make it clear that isolated incidents or over-zealousness of certain officials will in no way be allowed to mar the overall positive working environment for foreign investors."
Analysts said the Hubco incident was likely to be resolved but would be a blow to Pakistan's efforts to woo investment.

"Hubco has been the flagship project, the showpiece project of foreign interest in Pakistan. People equate Pakistan with Hubco. If you play around with Hubco it will have a serious impact," Rehman said.
Britain's National Power and Saudi Arabia's Xenel Industries Ltd have major stakes in the World Bank-backed $1.5 billion 1,292-megawatt Hubco plant that was completed in February.
Hubco's 10-rupee stock tumbled 0.55 rupee on Friday to close at 37350 at the Karachi Stock Exchange.
